lesson.title: Eight Is Enough: The Rule Behind Every Lewis Structure
lesson.summary: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons until they are surrounded by eight valence electrons, a stable arrangement that matches the electron configuration of a noble gas, and it is the target every Lewis structure is built around.
lesson.body:
Every Lewis structure drawn in the previous section was built toward the same invisible target: eight valence electrons around each atom. This target has a name, the octet rule, and it reflects a genuine physical fact, not just a bookkeeping convention. Atoms with eight valence electrons, an arrangement corresponding to a completely filled outer s and p subshell, are unusually low in energy and unusually unreactive, exactly the electron configuration found in every noble gas except helium. Atoms without a full octet are higher in energy and more reactive, so they gain, lose, or share electrons in whatever way gets them closer to that same stable arrangement, whether that means an ionic compound like sodium chloride, where sodium loses its one valence electron and chlorine gains one, or a covalent molecule like water, where oxygen and hydrogen each get to count shared electron pairs toward their own total.

Two elements follow a related but different target instead. Hydrogen and helium are far too small to hold eight electrons around them, since their entire outer shell is just the 1s orbital, which holds a maximum of two electrons. For these two elements, the stable target is a duet, not an octet, and hydrogen reaching two electrons by forming one bond, as it does in every one of its compounds, is playing by the same underlying logic as everything following the octet rule, just scaled down to the much smaller first shell.

The octet rule is a strong tendency, not an absolute law, and several genuine exceptions exist. Boron, and to a lesser extent aluminum, commonly forms compounds where the central atom ends up with only six electrons rather than eight, as in BF3, boron trifluoride, where boron has just three bonding pairs and no lone pair, an electron-deficient arrangement that is stable enough to exist but reactive enough to readily accept an additional electron pair from another molecule. At the other extreme, elements from period 3 onward, such as phosphorus and sulfur, can accommodate more than eight electrons around a central atom, called an expanded octet, because their larger size and available electron density let them support additional bonding pairs. Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5, has five bonding pairs around phosphorus, 10 electrons total, and sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, has six bonding pairs around sulfur, 12 electrons total, both perfectly stable, real compounds.

A third category of exception involves molecules with an odd total number of valence electrons, which makes a complete octet on every atom mathematically impossible, since electrons can only be grouped into full pairs on any single atom if the total is even to begin with. Nitric oxide, NO, has 11 total valence electrons, one atom is necessarily left with an unpaired electron, and the resulting species is called a free radical, generally more reactive than an equivalent molecule where every electron is paired.

Despite these exceptions, the octet rule remains the single most useful predictive tool for building correct Lewis structures across the overwhelming majority of molecules and ions a student encounters, precisely because it correctly identifies the electron count that minimizes energy for period 2 elements, which dominate the compounds of everyday chemistry, from water and carbon dioxide to the single and double bonds explored in the next two sections.
